title: Magnetically memorable inductance in superconducting multilayer resonators
authors: R. Tyumenev, D. S. Kalashnikov, B. V. Fradkin, A. A. Neilo, A. G. Shishkin, N. V. Klenov, I. I. Soloviev, A. A. Golubov, M. Yu. Kupriyanov, I. A. Golovchanskiy, V. S. Stolyarov, A. S. Sidorenko, S. V. Bakurskiy
abstract: Superconductor-ferromagnet hybrid structures with tunable kinetic inductance are promising elements for neuromorphic and quantum computing circuits. We report the fabrication and microwave characterization of split-ring resonators based on Nb/Co/Nb/Co/Nb/Al spin-trigger multilayers and demonstrate a non-volatile spin-valve effect on their resonant properties. Reversal of the relative magnetization orientation of the cobalt layers produces a reproducible shift of the resonant frequency up to 4 MHz at zero applied magnetic field, corresponding to a change in the kinetic inductance of the structure. The incorporation of a proximitized aluminum overlayer is shown to enhance the inductance contrast between the parallel and antiparallel magnetic states by a factor of approximately three relative to structures without this layer. The experimental results are in quantitative agreement with a microscopic model based on the Usadel equations. The demonstrated magnetic memory of the resonant frequency at zero field establishes spin-trigger multilayers as viable field-programmable inductive elements for superconducting digital and neuromorphic circuits.
summary: The authors fabricated superconducting multilayer resonators incorporating ferromagnetic layers to create magnetic memory elements. They experimentally demonstrated a non-volatile shift in the resonant frequency upon reversing the magnetization of the Co layers, confirming a spin-valve effect. This work establishes these structures as promising components for building tunable inductive circuits for neuromorphic and quantum computing applications.
main_problem: The research aims to demonstrate a non-volatile spin-valve effect on superconducting multilayer resonators, establishing them as viable field-programmable inductive elements for neuromorphic circuits.
main_result: A reproducible shift in the resonant frequency ($\Delta f$ up to 4 MHz) was observed upon magnetization reversal at zero applied magnetic field, confirming the magnetic memory of the structure.
method: Microwave characterization using transmission coefficient measurements ($S_{21}(f)$) on fabricated split-ring resonators (SRRs).
model_or_system: The physical platform is a superconducting multilayer resonator ($	ext{Nb}/	ext{Co}/	ext{Nb}/	ext{Co}/	ext{Nb}/	ext{Al}$) utilizing superconductor-ferromagnet hybrid structures. The physics is modeled using the Usadel equations.
key_observables: Resonant frequency shift ($\Delta f$), internal quality factor ($Q_i$), and kinetic inductance contrast between parallel and antiparallel magnetic states.
important_parameters: Operating temperature (2.5 K), resonant frequency range (4–7 GHz), and the magnitude of the frequency shift ($\sim 4 	ext{ MHz}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed effects are governed by changes in kinetic inductance due to magnetic state, and that the inclusion of an Al overlayer improves reproducibility.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate temperature dependence ($T$ vs $f_{	ext{res}}, Q_l$) and field dependence ($B$ vs $S_{21}, f_{	ext{res}}$), highlighting FMR anticrossings, sharp jumps at low fields, and the memory effect upon controlled magnetization reversal.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from demonstrating the basic spin-valve effect via frequency shifts to quantifying the enhancement provided by an aluminum shunt layer, comparing results against theoretical models (Usadel equations) and control samples.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges superconducting electronics with spintronics, creating tunable inductive elements whose state is controlled magnetically—a key concept for implementing artificial synapses in quantum/neuromorphic computing architectures.

A multilayer split-ring resonator (SRR) on a Si (100) substrate is placed on top of the central line of a planar waveguide (strip- line type). The external magnetic field B is applied along the waveguide. The top-left inset shows a cross-sectional sketch of the sample with the actual layer thicknesses. The bottom- right inset shows a photograph (top view) of the measured samples.

Figure 2. Temperature dependences of the parameters of the 4.7 GHz multilayer resonator. (a) Transmission coefficient S21 of the resonator at a fixed temperature of 2.5 K after background subtraction. The red curve shows a fit using the asymmetric Lorentzian profile (1). The resonator parameters obtained from the fit are indicated in the legend. (b) Temperature dependence of S21(f). (c) Resonant frequency and (d) internal quality factor of the resonator as functions of temperature.

Figure 3. Dependence of the parameters of the 4.7 GHz multilayer resonator on the external magnetic field. (a) Measured transmission coefficient S21 as a function of the magnetic field after background subtraction. The dotted-dashed line indicates the FMR dependence. (b) Resonant frequency and (d) internal quality factor, extracted using the fit from Eq. (1), as functions of the external magnetic field. The dashed line marks the field at which the thinner ferromagnetic layer reverses, resulting in an antiparallel configuration. (c) Resonant frequency and (e) internal quality factor in an expanded view of the region corresponding to the reversal of the thin layer.
